message.content:
The sea typically looks **blue**—the same reason we see the sky as blue. Sunlight contains all colors, but water absorbs longer wavelengths (red, orange) more strongly than shorter ones (green‑to‑violet). As a result, most of the visible spectrum reflected back from the surface is dominated by blues and greens.

However, what you actually perceive depends on several factors:

| Factor | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| Depth & clarity | Deeper, clearer waters look deeper blue; shallow or murky areas reflect more green or brown tones. |
| Algae / phytoplankton | High concentrations give a greenish tint. |
| Weather & lighting | Overcast skies reduce contrast, making the sea seem grayish or darker. |
| Surface waves | Breaking surf scatters light differently, sometimes giving a white or frothy appearance near shorelines. |

So while “blue” is the classic description, seas around the world can range from deep indigo to bright turquoise, even turning green or brown under certain natural circumstances.
